about: Paper 4 is a compulsory Part I paper in the Cambridge Economics Tripos that places economics in its political and social setting; the 2017 and 2019 editions of the University's Statutes and Ordinances title it 'Political and social aspects of economics'. A Varsity (student newspaper) report of 6 August 2026 says the Economics Faculty has proposed replacing the paper's two modules with 'Applied Social Science' and 'Economic and Social Data' and renaming the paper 'Applied Social Science'; we found no official notice confirming that the change, or any new title, has been adopted. The current syllabus and assessment are not published on any official page we could read, so this is a guide pack: it sets out what is confirmed and how to prepare, without inventing a syllabus.

notes.h: What Paper 4 is and how it has changed
notes.body:
Paper 4 is one of the five compulsory papers that every student takes in Part I (the first year) of the Cambridge Economics Tripos. The other four are Microeconomics (Paper 1), Macroeconomics (Paper 2), Quantitative Methods in Economics (Paper 3) and British economic history (Paper 5). Paper 4 is the paper that places economics in its political and social setting.

What the University's regulations say
- In the Statutes and Ordinances (for example the 2017 and 2019 editions) the paper is titled "Political and social aspects of economics".
- Its description says it considers how political and social factors influence economic affairs and how economics, politics and institutions are intertwined. It names post-war British economic and social policy-making and the politics of European Union integration, and also refers to political ideologies, domestic and international institutions, the nature of power in government, and wider social and economic processes.
- Some college admissions pages describe the paper more informally (one calls it "Sociology and Politics").

Recent and proposed changes
- According to a Varsity (student newspaper) report of 6 August 2026, the paper has recently been taught through two modules, "Governing Britain since 1945" and "Topics in Contemporary Political Economy", which the proposal would replace.
- The same report says the Faculty of Economics has proposed replacing these with two new modules, "Applied Social Science" and "Economic and Social Data", and renaming the paper "Applied Social Science". The Faculty said the redesign followed a year-long consultation and was intended to strengthen students' ability to apply economics to a broad range of social questions. The Cambridge Society for Economic Pluralism opposed the change and said students had been consulted too little; the Marshall Society welcomed the extra data science but asked for a clear rationale and consultation.
- At the time of the report the changes were proposals, not decisions, and the article did not say when they would take effect. Unizy lists this paper as "Economics and applied social science" as a working label only: it is not an official title, and we could not find an official page confirming any new title or the current syllabus.

What this means for you
- The content of Paper 4 in your year depends on whether, and when, the reform was adopted. Treat the paper guide, lecture list and Moodle pages issued by the Faculty in Michaelmas as the authority.
- Whatever the version, the paper's purpose is the same: to use economic reasoning, alongside evidence about politics, society and institutions, to analyse real policy questions. That shapes how you should prepare (see the other notes).

Because the current syllabus is not published anywhere we could read, this pack deliberately does not provide topic-by-topic notes. Inventing a syllabus would risk sending you to revise the wrong material.

notes.h: Assessment: what is and is not confirmed
notes.body:
The assessment details below are limited to what official University documents state. Paper 4's form of assessment may have changed with the recent reforms, so check the current arrangements.

Confirmed from the University's regulations
- Part I of the Economics Tripos consists of five papers, and every candidate must offer all of them.
- In the 2019 edition of the Statutes and Ordinances, Papers 1 to 4 of Part I were each set as three-hour written examinations. (Paper 5 had a different format: a two-hour paper plus project work.)

Not confirmed
- We could not find an official page giving the current format of Paper 4: for example, how many questions you answer, whether there is any coursework or data exercise, or how the two modules are weighted. If the proposed "Economic and Social Data" module has been introduced, it is possible that part of the paper is assessed differently, but this is speculation and you should not rely on it.
- Do not rely on older past papers alone if the syllabus has changed; questions on topics such as post-war British governance would not appear if those modules have been replaced.

Where to find the definitive information
- The Faculty of Economics' Part I paper guide or outline for Paper 4, issued at the start of the year (usually on Moodle).
- Notices of the form and conduct of examinations, published in the Cambridge University Reporter (these are how the University announces changes such as new coursework components).
- Your Director of Studies and supervisors, who will know how the paper is currently examined.
- The Faculty's past examination papers archive, used with care if the syllabus has changed.

Practical points that apply in any case
- Cambridge examinations are marked against published classing criteria; answers that are relevant, well structured and supported by evidence and analysis score highest.
- In timed essay papers, planning matters: allocate time in proportion to marks and leave time to check that each answer addresses the question asked.

Because the detailed syllabus may have changed, prepare in a way that works whichever version of Paper 4 you sit, and then follow the Faculty's reading lists closely once you have them.

Skills that the paper rewards in any version
- Applying economic reasoning to social and political questions. Practise taking a policy issue (for example housing, welfare, education, regional inequality or trade) and asking: what are the incentives, who gains and loses, what institutions shape the outcome, and what does the evidence show?
- Using evidence. Distinguish correlation from causation, ask how a statistic was measured, and be cautious about drawing strong conclusions from a single study or chart.
- Writing analytical essays. Answer the question set, define key terms, build an argument rather than a list, consider counter-arguments and reach a justified conclusion.

If the paper includes political economy and British policy history
- Build a timeline of major post-war economic policy decisions and the debates around them, and link each to economic reasoning from Papers 1 and 2.
- Use your supervisors' reading lists rather than general textbooks, as essay questions are set on the lecture content.

If the paper includes applied social science or economic and social data
- Make sure your statistics from Paper 3 are secure: descriptive statistics, sampling, regression and interpreting coefficients.
- Get familiar with the main sources of UK economic and social data (for example the Office for National Statistics) and with reading tables and charts critically.
- Practise explaining what a dataset can and cannot tell you about a policy question.

Weekly routine
- After each lecture, write a one-page summary in your own words with the key arguments, authors and evidence.
- Treat supervision essays as exam practice: plan in 10 minutes, write in timed conditions occasionally, and act on feedback.
- Keep a list of short, accurate examples (with dates and sources) that you can use across questions.

In the Easter Term
- Check the confirmed format for your year, collect the past questions that match your syllabus, and practise full timed answers.
- Revise across the whole paper rather than question-spotting, since the choice of questions can vary from year to year.

Unizy will add topic-by-topic notes for this paper once its current syllabus is published on an official page.
